evidence.title: A geometry and dose-volume based performance monitoring of artificial intelligence models in radiotherapy treatment planning for prostate cancer
evidence.venue: Physics and imaging in radiation oncology
evidence.outcome: Detection of out-of-distribution planning inputs using volume and clinical-goal analysis
evidence.effect: Training versus local volumes: PTV (154 ± 45)cm 3 versus (120 ± 50)cm 3; bladder (141 ± 51)cm 3 versus (226 ± 136)cm 3; both p < 0.001.
evidence.quote: The geometrical analysis showed significant volume differences between the training and the local dataset for respectively PTV ((154 ± 45)cm 3 ; (120 ± 50)cm 3 with p < 0.001), bladder ((141 ± 51)cm 3 ; (226 ± 136)cm 3 with p < 0.001) and rectum ((58 ± 18)cm 3 ; (76 ± 29)cm 3 with p < 0.001).

evidence.title: Evolution of an Artificial Intelligence-Powered Application for Mammography
evidence.outcome: Monthly technical monitoring of missing or incomplete AI outputs
evidence.effect: Defects (no output or incomplete image analysis) exceeded the 10% threshold several times. The average defect proportion declined from 9.0% to 1.0% after feedback-driven fixes.
evidence.quote: The average proportion of technical defects declined from 9.0% to 1.0%, while the clinical assessment score improved from 63.4 to 72.0.

evidence.title: A Two-Phase Framework Leveraging User Feedback and Systemic Validation to Improve Post-Live Clinical Decision Support
evidence.outcome: Detection of post-live CDS malfunctions via data flow and rules validation
evidence.effect: Seven types of malfunctions identified over 2 years in 14 facilities; general malfunction rate below 2%; framework captured low-prevalence malfunctions.
evidence.quote: It provides objective insights into the extent of CDS issues, with the ability to capture low-prevalence malfunctions.

evidence.title: Establishing prospective performance monitoring for real-world implementation of deep learning-based auto-segmentation in prostate cancer radiotherapy
evidence.venue: Physics and imaging in radiation oncology
evidence.outcome: Flagging of out-of-distribution outlier cases (e.g., metal artifacts)
evidence.effect: Flagged prostate outliers included 5 cases with fiducials and 6 with hip implants; rectum, bladder, femoral head outliers attributed to metal artifacts and generalization limits.
evidence.quote: By employing statistical process control, our framework effectively identified out-of-distribution outliers, serving as an early warning mechanism to prevent performance degradation.

evidence.title: Validation is not enough: Longitudinal evidence of post-deployment fragility in clinical AI systems
evidence.outcome: Association and temporal precedence of input missingness/latency with calibration degradation
evidence.effect: Missingness βstd -0.42 to -0.21 across systems; negative in 12/12 specifications; telemetry ΔR² 0.21–0.28 vs population 0.05–0.07; temporal ordering preserved in all leave-one-out analyses.
evidence.quote: Input missingness and data latency preserved negative associations with calibration slope in all tested specifications.
evidence.sample_unit: deployed AI systems (1,814,000 inference events total)

evidence.title: Ensuring fair, safe, and interpretable artificial intelligence-based prediction tools in a real-world oncological setting
evidence.outcome: Detection of data pipeline failures via prediction volume and PSI monitoring
evidence.effect: Leading indicators (prediction volume drop, PSI spike) detected a 2-week EHR API/data feed outage causing incomplete inputs; issue quickly resolved; would likely not be caught by performance monitoring alone.
evidence.quote: We note that this issue would likely not have been noticed if we were monitoring for model performance alone.

evidence.title: Self-supervised out-of-distribution detection-Metal implants and other anomaly
evidence.outcome: Detection of anomalous/out-of-distribution CT inputs in prospective and external test sets
evidence.effect: Prospective TP rate 86.11% despite under-documentation of anomalies in reports; external AbdominalCT-1k TP rate 75.26% with 24.7% FP rate, mostly from anomalies outside the body.
evidence.quote: Prospective analysis showed the model was able to handle the under-documentation of anomaly in radiology reports with 86.11% true positive (TP) rate.

evidence.title: Importance of model governance in clinical AI models: case study on the relevance of data drift detection
evidence.outcome: Whether input data monitoring detects anomalous values and data pipeline integrity issues
evidence.effect: PCA reconstruction error flagged data entry errors (saturation '955' instead of '95', incorrect heart rate) and an outlier length of stay; after pipeline modification, alerts for those months were removed.
evidence.quote: After modifying the data pipeline to guard against these types of data entry errors, the multivariate alerts for these months were removed.

evidence.title: A quality assurance framework for routine monitoring of deep learning cardiac substructure computed tomography segmentation models in radiotherapy
evidence.outcome: Ability of input image and output shape detectors to identify abnormal domains and predict segmentation performance
evidence.effect: Linear regression with bagging achieved MAE 0.041 ± 0.002 in predicted DSC; MAE was lowest when combining input (image) and output (shape) detectors compared to output detectors alone.
evidence.quote: MAE was lowest when combining both input (image) detectors and output (shape) detectors compared to output detectors alone.

evidence.title: Distribution shift detection for the postmarket surveillance of medical AI algorithms: a retrospective simulation study
evidence.outcome: out-of-distribution input shift detection
evidence.effect: OOD low-quality shift: all methods had perfect test power with 100 training examples; test sample m = 50 for C2ST/MUKS and m = 200 for MMDD.
evidence.quote: For such a shift, all methods reached perfect test power with only 100 training examples, and even the test sample size could be reduced drastically to ca. m = 50 for C2ST and MUKS and m = 200 for MMDD.

evidence.title: One-class support vector machines for detecting population drift in deployed machine learning medical diagnostics
evidence.outcome: Share of simulated drifted records flagged as outliers versus inliers by OCSVM at three noise levels
evidence.effect: Records misclassified as inliers: 27/10,000 (0.27%) at 5% noise, 486 (4.86%) at 10%, 851 (8.51%) at 30%. Most drifted records were flagged, but detection fell as overlap with training data grew.
evidence.quote: At the lowest noise level (5%), the model classified 27 records as inliers (27 out of 10,000).

evidence.title: Dimensionality Reduction for Improving Out-of-Distribution Detection in Medical Image Segmentation
evidence.venue: Uncertainty for safe utilization of machine learning in medical imaging : 5th international workshop, UNSURE 2023, held in conjunction with MICCAI 2023, Vancouver, BC, Canada, October 12, 2023, proceedings. UNSURE (Workshop) (5th : 2023
evidence.outcome: Out-of-distribution image detection at inference for a deployed segmentation model
evidence.effect: Post hoc Mahalanobis distance with PCA detected failed images with 92% AUROC and 94% AUPRC.
evidence.quote: By reducing the dimensions of the bottleneck features with principal component analysis, images the model failed on were detected with high performance and minimal computational load.

evidence.title: Dimensionality Reduction and Nearest Neighbors for Improving Out-of-Distribution Detection in Medical Image Segmentation
evidence.venue: The journal of machine learning for biomedical imaging
evidence.outcome: Out-of-distribution failure detection
evidence.effect: Images the models failed on were detected with high performance and minimal computational load; no numbers reported.
evidence.quote: By reducing the dimensions of the bottleneck features with either principal component analysis or uniform manifold approximation and projection, images the models failed on were detected with high performance and minimal computational load.

evidence.title: Quantifying Epistemic Uncertainty in Predictions for Safer Health AI Performance Under Dataset Shifts
evidence.venue: Studies in health technology and informatics
evidence.outcome: Whether uncertainty screening flags out-of-distribution samples that drive prediction errors
evidence.effect: Sample-level epistemic uncertainty threshold flagged potential OOD samples and captured most prediction errors, with no retraining required.
evidence.quote: Results across all training-test time pairs show that samples below this threshold exhibit consistently higher macro-F1 and render performance virtually invariant to temporal drift, while the flagged samples captured most prediction errors.

evidence.title: Impact of labelling inaccuracy and image noise on tooth segmentation in panoramic radiographs using federated, centralized, and local learning
evidence.outcome: Whether per-client loss trajectory monitoring detects corrupted data from a faulty site
evidence.effect: Loss curve monitoring reliably flagged the corrupted site in label and image-noise corruption scenarios.
evidence.quote: Loss curve monitoring reliably flagged the corrupted site.

evidence.title: Preserving Informative Presence: How Missing Data and Imputation Strategies Affect the Performance of an AI-Based Early Warning Score
evidence.outcome: AUROC of early warning score under missing inputs and forced imputation
evidence.effect: AUROC 0.918 with actual data fell to 0.883 with mean-based imputation and 0.827 with MICE; specificity at 80% sensitivity fell from 85.5% to 78.3%.
evidence.quote: When missing values were imputed using values randomly drawn from within one SD of the mean observed values for the corresponding non-event and event groups, the AUROC decreased to 0.883 (95% CI: 0.875–0.891) compared with 0.918 (95% CI: 0.912–0.924) under the model’s default normal-value imputation method (DeLong test, p < 0.001).

evidence.title: Implementation of an artificial intelligence-based system for mammography in the compulsory medical insurance program: results of a 3-year study
evidence.venue: Quantitative imaging in medicine and surgery
evidence.outcome: Automatically logged technical defect (analysis failure) rates during prospective monitoring
evidence.effect: Technical defects exceeded 10% in 1 of 25 months (11.10%); average defect rate decreased from 3.0% to 0.8%.
evidence.quote: Technical defect rates exceeded 10% in only 1 of 25 months (group B defects: 11.10%; Figure 3A ).

evidence.title: Evolution of an Artificial Intelligence-Powered Application for Mammography
evidence.outcome: Technical defects over time
evidence.effect: Technical monitoring detected instances where technical defects, such as incomplete image analysis or missing outputs, exceeded the 10% threshold.
evidence.quote: The technical defect monitoring plot highlights several instances where the technical defects exceeded the established threshold ( Figure 6 a).

evidence.title: A Case Report in Using a Laboratory-Based Decision Support Alert for Research Enrollment and Randomization
evidence.outcome: Technical failures of laboratory input data pipeline preventing the CDS alert from firing
evidence.effect: Laboratory vendor change, a broken lab machine, and a lab test name change prevented the alert from firing; 3,961 assessed, 2,105 randomized.
evidence.quote: Technical challenges that prevented the custom CDS alert from firing included an unanticipated change in the laboratory testing vendor and reporting due to a broken laboratory machine, followed by a change in the laboratory test name.

evidence.title: Establishing prospective performance monitoring for real-world implementation of deep learning-based auto-segmentation in prostate cancer radiotherapy
evidence.venue: Physics and imaging in radiation oncology
evidence.outcome: Segmentation outliers associated with image artifacts and implanted materials
evidence.effect: Among prostate outliers, five cases were associated with fiducials and six with hip implants. Many other patients with fiducials remained within acceptable thresholds; hip-prosthesis metal artifacts also contributed to femoral-head segmentation failures.
evidence.quote: Among the prostate outliers, five cases were associated with fiducials and six with hip implants.

evidence.title: Validation is not enough: Longitudinal evidence of post-deployment fragility in clinical AI systems
evidence.outcome: effect of data missingness on calibration
evidence.effect: input missingness and data latency were strongly associated with declining calibration
evidence.quote: Input missingness and data latency were most strongly associated with declining calibration slope in Systems A and B.

evidence.title: Unsupervised out-of-distribution detection for safer robotically guided retinal microsurgery
evidence.venue: International journal of computer assisted radiology and surgery
evidence.outcome: Downstream model performance on corrupted or out-of-distribution input data without detection
evidence.effect: Without rejection, corrupted A-scans are processed by the retinal network, and the Raw-MahaAD, Glow, Uncertainty, and SNR detectors underperformed the No-rejection baseline.
evidence.quote: Raw-MahaAD , Glow , Uncertainty , and SNR underperformed compared to No-rejection , suggesting that they flag a large proportion of correct samples as OoD while allowing corrupted A-scans to be processed by the subsequent retinal network.
evidence.sample_unit: M-scans (258 real OoD and 258 in-distribution) in the real-OoD test; 2,000 M-scans in the simulated-corruption test

evidence.title: Towards reliable WMH segmentation under domain shift: An application study using maximum entropy regularization to improve uncertainty estimation
evidence.outcome: Model calibration and segmentation quality under MRI domain shift
evidence.effect: Domain shifts such as MRI machine type or acquisition parameters pose significant challenges to model calibration and uncertainty estimation; no numeric results reported in the abstract.
evidence.quote: However, domain shifts, such as variations in MRI machine types or acquisition parameters, pose significant challenges to model calibration and uncertainty estimation.

evidence.title: Lightweight and interpretable edge intelligence AI with intrusion detection for trustworthy cardiac arrhythmia in medical IoT
evidence.outcome: Detection of unreliable or attacked ECG inputs via attack probability and trust score
evidence.effect: Intrusion detection module outputs an attack probability and trust score flagging unreliable inputs; generalization under dataset shift reported as AUC 0.940 on PTB-XL and 0.915 on Chapman (zero-shot).
evidence.quote: To improve trust under hostile network conditions, an intrusion detection module outputs an attack probability and a trust score that flags unreliable inputs.

evidence.title: Robustness of Healthcare ML Under Data Quality Degradation: A Dimension-Wise Analysis on MIMIC-IV
evidence.venue: Studies in health technology and informatics
evidence.outcome: Model performance under controlled missing, incoherent, invalid, imprecise and duplicate data at inference time
evidence.effect: Performance declined with increasing degradation, with largest losses when degradations occurred at inference time. Completeness, coherence and validity were the most detrimental dimensions.
evidence.quote: Model performance declined with increasing degradation, with the largest losses observed when degradations occurred at inference time.

evidence.title: Impact of Data Quality Degradation on the Robustness of Clinical Regression Models: A Study on ICU Length of Stay
evidence.venue: Studies in health technology and informatics
evidence.outcome: Regression error when evaluation inputs had missing, incoherent, invalid, imprecise or duplicated data
evidence.effect: Models trained on clean data showed consistently rising prediction error as input data quality degraded, with coherence degradation most harmful.
evidence.quote: Prediction error increases consistently with degradation, with coherence having the strongest impact, in line with clinical intuition.

evidence.title: How data drift impacts the safety and interpretability of machine learning models predicting risk from blood glucose control
evidence.outcome: Effect of anomalous or shifted input data on model outputs and covariate shift detection
evidence.effect: Even 5% noise gave normalised JS divergence of 172 sigma; sensor noise and offsets degraded performance and changed output rates.
evidence.quote: Even a modest addition of 5% noise leads to a very significant covariate shift.
evidence.sample_unit: adults with type 1 diabetes (REPLACE trial CGM data)

commentary.bottom_line: Fifteen observational, simulated, or benchmark studies report that input and output data checks detected missing outputs, pipeline outages, data entry errors, and out-of-distribution cases, and one deployment saw average defects fall from 9.0% to 1.0% after feedback-driven fixes. No study measured whether these checks reduced patient harm, and none compared sites with and without monitoring.

perspectives.view: Five level 3 studies came from real deployments, and ten were offline, simulated, or benchmark tests. None was randomized, and none had a concurrent control. Every study reported that checks detected data problems, so the findings are consistent. The outcomes were detection rates and defect counts rather than patient outcomes, which lowers directness.

Hazard studies show the failure is real. AUROC fell from 0.918 to 0.827 under imputation, and lab pipeline changes stopped an alert from firing. Leading indicators caught a 2-week data feed outage that performance monitoring alone would likely have missed. No study traced a detected failure to harm that was prevented.

Across 14 facilities over 2 years, data flow validation found seven malfunction types at rates below 2%. In another study, PCA reconstruction error flagged entry errors such as saturation recorded as 955. One external test produced a 24.7% false positive rate, which suggests alert burden may be a problem if thresholds are not tuned locally.

In four deployed systems, missingness and latency telemetry explained more calibration change (ΔR² 0.21 to 0.28) than population factors did (0.05 to 0.07). This suggests low-cost telemetry may give early warning. In a mammography program, defects fell from 3.0% to 0.8%. No study reported staffing or cost.

One benchmark used retinal images from a sample focused on racial and ethnic minority groups, and one CT study included older adults. Neither reported results by insurance, language, or literacy. Out-of-distribution detection may flag patients whose data differ from the training data, but no study examined whether flagging rates differed across groups.

FDA draft guidance on AI-enabled device software lists missing values, duplicate records, and data type mismatches as quality concerns, with permissive (may) language. CHAI's assurance guide frames data quality monitoring as a must. No supplied study evaluated compliance with, or the effect of, either document.

Flagged radiotherapy outliers included 5 patients with fiducials and 6 with hip implants. This suggests patients with implanted devices may be more likely to receive faulty AI contours. The studies did not report whether flagged cases went to a human reviewer or whether patients were told.

commentary.research_gap: No study compared patient outcomes, missed-error rates, or clinician workload between settings with and without routine data checks. Thresholds, false alert rates in live use, staffing needs, and costs remain unmeasured.
commentary.underserved_note: No test included Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. One benchmark had a racial and ethnic minority focus, and one CT study included older adults. Health systems serving these groups cannot yet know whether monitoring detects failures in their data at the reported rates.
